genZNote: Fermented the acetone that helped make WWI-era explosives (via the ABE process) — one of the earliest large-scale industrial fermentation success stories, decades before 'biotech' was a word.

morphology.notes: Forms oval, subterminal endospores, often giving sporulating cells a swollen 'clostridial' appearance.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, decaying plant material, and the intestinal tracts of some animals
habitat.hostAssociation: Free-living environmental organism, not typically a human pathogen
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Widespread in soil worldwide; historically cultured industrially at massive scale for solvent production

microscopy.appearance: Gram-positive rods with oval subterminal endospores

culture.growthCharacteristics: Strict anaerobe; ferments carbohydrates to acetone, butanol, and ethanol (the ABE fermentation)
culture.colonyMorphology: Irregular, spreading colonies under strict anaerobic culture

identificationClues: Strict anaerobe forming characteristic oval, subterminal endospores that swell the sporulating cell
Ferments sugars via the acetone-butanol-ethanol (ABE) pathway, historically used for large-scale industrial acetone and butanol production
Named the 'Weizmann organism' after Chaim Weizmann, who developed the industrial ABE fermentation process in the early 20th century
Not considered a human pathogen, unlike several other well-known Clostridium species

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: The 'Weizmann organism' behind the historic industrial acetone-butanol-ethanol fermentation process

sources.name: NCBI Bookshelf — overview of Clostridium species and industrial fermentation history
